chunks: From him, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurarah, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), that he was asked:

About a man whose prayer time entered while he was traveling, so he delayed the prayer until he arrived home, intending to pray it when he reached his family. He forgot to pray it upon arrival until the time had passed. He said: 'He prays it two rak'at as the prayer of the traveler, because the time entered while he was a traveler, so it was incumbent upon him to pray at that time.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a traveler who delays his prayer until arriving home and forgets to pray it until the time expires?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) establishes that the obligation to shorten the prayer (qasr) is fixed by the state of travel at the onset of the prayer time, meaning the traveler remains entitled to two rak'at even if he delays until returning home and subsequently forgets. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic principle that the legal status of the prayer is determined by the condition present when the time begins, rather than the condition at the moment of actual performance. It underscores the flexibility granted to travelers, ensuring that the concession of qasr is not lost due to minor delays or forgetfulness upon arrival.
